newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel turns to U.S., Egypt as Hebron seethes.
newsitem.headline: Israel turns to U.S., Egypt as Hebron seethes.

text.p: Israel tried on Thursday to enlist U.S. and Egyptian support for its efforts to pressure Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority to quell outbreaks of violence in the West Bank tinderbox of Hebron.
Israeli troops wounded three Palestinians in clashes on Thursday in Hebron, where undercover soldiers posing as Arabs arrested young protesters in the West Bank town, witnesses said.
Israeli gunfire and Palestinian petrol bombs and stones have peppered the town since a Jewish woman ignited Arab anger by posting placards mocking the Prophet Mohammad at the weekend.
Israel laid the blame for the unrest squarely at the door of the Palestinian Authority, warning the self-rule body to quash the violence or risk a stronger military response.
"We can use a lot of power which we don't want to use," Israel's Hebron military commander, identified only as Colonel Gadi, told Reuters. "We haven't used even five percent of our power in Hebron."
Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai on Thursday met U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and Egypt's envoy Mohammad Bassiouny to discuss the Hebron bloodshed.

"In the three-way meeting the defence minister made clear to the two ambassadors the security establishment's position that the Palestinian Authority is under the obligation to deal with the rioting in Hebron with an iron fist," Mordechai's office said in a statement.
But Egypt, main mediator of the troubled peace process, said on Thursday it was up to Israel to change its policies if Cairo's efforts to revive the talks were to bear fruit.
The talks collapsed in March, after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline government enraged Arabs by breaking ground on a new settlement in East Jerusalem.
The Hebron clashes on Thursday began near the Jewish enclave of Beit Hadassah on the Israeli-held side of the West Bank town, divided since January under a peace deal with the PLO.
Undercover soldiers had mingled with a morning crowd of about 50 youths in Hebron, speaking Arabic, dressing like Arabs in plain clothes, and wearing masks and keffiyeh headdresses.

When the Palestinians began throwing stones at uniformed troops and burning an Israeli flag, the undercover men began beating and pushing them, even dragging one along the ground, while making about six arrests, witnesses said.
After being surprised by the undercover soldiers, the protesters retreated to the Palestinian-held side but continued to stone troops on the Israeli side.

The soldiers responded by firing rubber bullets while Israeli snipers armed with live ammunition deployed on roofs for a second day. Hospital officials said the wounded Palestinians, hit by rubber-coated metal bullets, were not seriously hurt.

Tatyana Suskin, a 26-year-old Jewish woman from Jerusalem, was charged on Thursday with illegally posting placards that depicted Prophet Mohammad as a pig on some 20 Hebron storefronts on Friday, and with endangering life by stoning an Arab car on Saturday. The offences carry a 24-year maximum sentence.
In Wednesday unrest sparked by anger over the posters, troops wounded 37 youths in protests in Hebron and shot dead an Arab teenager in a clash in Gaza on Wednesday.
Netanyahu would give no ground on the roots of the unrest.

"This is not spontaneous violence with one or two exceptions. It is organised by the Palestinian Authority and in those cases where it's not organised by the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian police sit back and do nothing to stop this," Netanyahu told reporters.

Palestinian security sources in Hebron said Ibrahim Ghneimat, a top member of a Hamas military cell that carried out several attacks against Israelis, escaped from a PLO prison in Hebron and police were searching for him.

Ghneimat was among several Hamas guerrillas rounded up by Israel and the Palestinian Authority in April after a bombing in Tel Aviv in March in which three Israeli women were killed. The cell also kidnapped and killed an Israeli soldier.
Israeli security authorities cast doubt on the reports of an escape. "I tend to think he was released," Gadi said.
